items.translation_text: Modern Translation: We leave it to the pious and attentive reader to consider how much should be attributed to those epistles. For we do not doubt that in reading them these things will come to anyone's mind; first, that in almost all the epistles, though very copious, the occasion of writing is omitted, nor can one even guess why he chiefly wished to send letters to this or that church. Secondly, the logic of his journey itself injects no small scruple to those considering it, because by a much straighter and shorter journey he could have sailed to Rome, as even the example of Paul himself testifies. Consider how long a journey it is, to withdraw from Antioch to the shore of the Aegean sea, and there straight upwards towards the North to ascend, and survey the chief cities situated on the shore as far as Troas, when nevertheless the Roman journey is destined towards the setting sun. Thirdly, things of such a kind are interspersed in those letters that the reader is almost astounded at them, etc. Since these things, along with others, fall upon a reader who is not asleep, we would not have thought... (Magdeburg Centuriators, Centuriae Magdeburgenses, )

items.exact_text: cur huic donetur perseverantia, usque in finem, illi non donetur, inscrutabilia sunt judicia Dei: illud tamen fidelibus debet ease certissimum, hunt ease ex praedestinatis, illum non ease: ' Nam si fuiasent ex nobis' (air unus praedestinatorum qui e pectore Domini biberat hoc secretum) 'mansiasent utique nobiscum.' Quae est ista discretio? Patent libri Dei, non avertamus aspectum, clamat Scriptura Divina, adhibeamus auditum, non erant ex eis, quia non erant secundum propesitum vocati: non erant in Christo electi ante mundi constitutionem, non erant in eo sortem consecuti, non erant praedestinati secundum propositum ejus qui omnia operatur.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: Why perseverance to the end is given to this one, and not given to that one, the judgments of God are unsearchable: yet it ought to be most certain to believers, that the former is of the predestinated, the latter is not: 'For if they had been of us' (says one of the predestinated who had drunk this secret from the Lord's breast) 'they would no doubt have continued with us.' What is this distinction? The books of God are open, let us not turn away our gaze; the Divine Scripture cries out, let us apply our hearing: they were not of them, because they were not called according to the purpose: they were not chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, they had not obtained an inheritance in Him, they were not predestinated according to the purpose of Him who works all things. (Augustine, De Correptione et Gratia, Chapter 8)

items.exact_text: Electi quippe sic ad bonum tendunt, ut ad mala perpetranda non redeant; et, potest discursus, et mobilitas spiritus sic intelligi. In sanctorum quippe cordibus juxta quasdam virtutes semper permanet; juxta quasdam vero recessurus venit, venturus recedit: in fide etenim, et spe, et charitate, et bonis aliis, sine quibus ad coelestem patriam non potest veniri (sicut est humilitas, castitas, justitia, atque misericordia) perfectorum corda non deserit: in prophetiae vero virtute, doctrinae facundia, miraculorum exhibitione, suls aliquando adest, aliquando se subtrahit.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: The elect indeed so tend to good, that they do not return to committing evil; and the discursion and mobility of the spirit can be thus understood. In the hearts of the saints, according to some virtues he always remains; but according to some he comes about to depart, and departs about to come: for in faith, and hope, and charity, and other goods, without which one cannot come to the heavenly country (such as humility, chastity, justice, and mercy) he does not desert the hearts of the perfect: but in the virtue of prophecy, the eloquence of doctrine, the exhibition of miracles, he is sometimes present to his own, and sometimes withdraws himself. (Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job, Book 2)

items.exact_text: De praedestinatis verum est infallibiliter, quod gratiam finaliter seu in perpetuum non amittunt; unde postquam semel gratiam habuerant, ita reguntur et proteguntur a Deo, ut vel non cadant, vel si deciderint resurgant; et licet saepius cadant et resurgant, tandem aliquando ita resurgunt ut amplius non cadant.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: It is infallibly true of the predestined, that they do not lose grace finally or perpetually; whence after they have once had grace, they are so governed and protected by God, that either they do not fall, or if they have fallen they rise again; and although they may fall and rise again frequently, at last they rise again in such a way that they fall no more. (Unknown Scholastic, Unknown Work, Unknown Location)

items.exact_text: Quod nomen perseverantiae nullam rein absolutam essentialiter significat, sed accidentaliter et relative; charitatem videlicet, sire justitiam cure respectu futurae permansionis usque in finem, et quod non improbabiliter posset dici perseverantiam esse ipsam relationem hujus.
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: That the name of perseverance essentially signifies no absolute thing, but accidentally and relatively; namely, charity or righteousness with respect to a future continued remaining unto the end; and that it might not improbably be said that perseverance is the very relation thereof. (Thomas Bradwardine, De Causa Dei contra Pelagium, Book II, Chapter VII)

items.exact_text: "Quidam sunt, qui jam aliquamdiu luce veritatis collustrati fuerunt, et in ejus cognitione pietatisque studio tantum profecerunt, ut habitum tandem credendi sancteque vivendi comparaverint: hos non tantum ad finem usque vitae perseverare posse, seal facile posse, ac libenter et cum voluptate perseverare velle credimus, adeo ut non nisi cum lucta et molestia ac difficultate deficere Possint." — Act. Synod. Dec. Sent. A. 5, pp. 189, 190.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “There are some who have already for some time been illuminated by the light of truth, and have made such progress in the knowledge thereof and in the study of piety, that they have at length acquired a habit of believing and living holily: these, we believe, are not only able to persevere to the very end of life, but are easily able, and willingly and with pleasure desire to persevere, to such a degree that they cannot fall away unless with struggle, trouble, and difficulty.”

items.exact_text: "Hunc Ezechielis locum saris commode explicat Erasmus in sua Diatribe, dicens, In eo contineri usitatam figuram loquendi, qua cura in altero aliquid efficiendi significatur, illius opera minime exclusa: ac si quis (inquit) praeceptor discipulo soloecizanti diceret, Exeram tibi linguam istam barbaricam, et inseram Romanam. Haec sunt fere ipsius Erasmi verba. Quibus adde ex loco ipso saris apparere nullam necessitatem Deum significare voluisse, seal neque ullam vim interiorem, cum non alia ratione ea, quae ibi pollicetur se effecturum, ostendat Deus, quam beneficiorum multitudine, quibus affecturus erat populum, ejusque cor et animum emolliturus," etc. — Soc. Prael. cap. 12 s. 6, p. 45.
items.modern_reference: Translation: “Erasmus explains this passage of Ezekiel quite suitably in his Diatribe, saying that it contains a common figure of speech, by which care in effecting something in another is signified, not at all excluding the other's own effort: as if (he says) a teacher were to say to a pupil making grammatical errors, ‘I will draw out of you that barbarous tongue, and implant the Roman.’ These are almost the very words of Erasmus himself. To which add, that from the passage itself it sufficiently appears that God did not wish to signify any necessity, nor indeed any internal force, since God does not show that he will effect those things which he there promises in any other way than by a multitude of benefits, with which he was about to affect the people, and to soften their heart and mind,” etc.

items.exact_text: {Ολως seems to be a misprint for ὄντως, which is the reading of the textus receptus. This latter reading is now abandoned in the critical editions of the New Testament. Estius seems to have adopted ὀλίγον? Bloomfield has no doubt that it should be ὀλίγω? Tischendorf, on the authority of some of the most ancient manuscripts, several ancient versions, and several of the Fathers, inserts ὀλίγως in the text as the proper reading. The meaning in this case would be "almost." In the translation of De Wette, "beinahe," "almost," is the word employed. — ED.
